newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: WHO links environment and illness -- vaguely.
newsitem.headline: WHO links environment and illness -- vaguely.

text.p: The World Health Organisation said on Wednesday that environmental factors were to blame for as much as a quarter of all preventable illnesses, but included workplace incidents and even traffic accidents among them.
Officials of the Geneva-based United Nations agency were unveiling a new report on links between health and environment ahead of Monday's world environmental summit in New York.
WHO said one billion people were exposed to severe air pollution and one million people died each year because of it.

Executive director Wilfried Kreisel said poor environmental quality was directly responsible for 25 percent of all preventable human illnesses, with diarrhoeal diseases and respiratory infections heading the list.
But the report was full of generalisations that made it hard to establish clear causal links between illness and the environment.
Kreisel said deaths and injuries caused by road traffic accidents around the world had been included in WHO's count of illnesses caused by environmental factors, but did not elaborate.

He said the count also included mental disorders, which accounted for 10 percent of the total burden of disease. But he provided no links to specific environmental problems apart from saying that "chemical explosions" affected the brain.

Tord Kjellstrom, a senior WHO official, said 125 million workplace injuries each year, including those from lifting heavy objects, had also been counted among environment-related diseases because "the workplace is a dangerous environment".
But he gave no breakdown of injuries in highly polluted or environmentally hazardous areas such as oil refining, toxic chemicals or nuclear plants.
Critics accuse WHO and several other U.N. agencies of exaggerating problems in their efforts to raise funds. Last week, WHO issued a statement describing obesity as an epidemic.
Insiders also say the agencies often stick to generalisations for fear of angering member states with hard-hitting comments.
WHO helped to alert the world to the spread of AIDS, and worked to eradicate polio in the Western hemisphere.

But advocates of U.N. reform now single it out as one agency in urgent need of restructuring. They say WHO needs to reform its unwieldy, top-heavy bureaucracy to focus better on its role of promoting global health issues, setting standards and providing advice and information.

Like many other U.N. agencies in Geneva, WHO operates independently of the world body's New York headquarters and diplomats say the reform-minded U.N. Secretary General, Kofi Annan, has little direct authority over it.
